source.title: Towards Combinatorial Interpretability of Neural Computation
source.authors: Micah Adler; Dan Alistarh; N. Shavit

page_placements.theme: Capacity limits and computation in superposition (theory and constructions)

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses a different, static analysis of signed weights to study feature coding and polysemanticity in trained networks.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports results on Boolean-task accuracy, formula reconstruction, and code-based classification. I include results where they bear on feature overlap, polysemanticity, or the relation between coding and capacity; task-performance results that do not measure those properties are not included.
record.test_reason: In small gradient-trained Boolean MLPs, the paper reports polysemantic neurons where features number fewer than neurons (8 clauses on 16 neurons). It argues that polysemanticity also appears when the network does not need superposition. That bears directly on V4 and qualifies V3 as a general cause. The clause-sweep scaling results measure coding capacity and training error, not polysemanticity.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right. The authors propose feature-channel coding, in which shared cross-neuron codes make neurons polysemantic. They report polysemanticity even when features are fewer than neurons, and hypothesize, untested, that gradient descent favors the more numerous overlapping-code minima. They also report that their networks do not reach superposition: error starts once clauses roughly equal hidden width, because 4P codes can no longer be packed in.
record.recipe_differences: The paper analyzes signs and combinatorial patterns in trained weight matrices for small Boolean tasks rather than measuring image-neuron responses or using the original sources' methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported coding and error outcomes vary with clause count and hidden-layer width.

fits_no_version.finding: Training error begins when clause count reaches hidden width (j=16, 32, 64). It tracks the fall of 4P coding patterns per clause below about 1.5–2, matching a packing bound of roughly jℓ/(16k). The networks do not compute more features than neurons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In small Boolean MLPs, accuracy breaks down when the number of features exceeds the combinatorial capacity for feature-channel codes, roughly when features exceed neurons.

record.problems: Evidence concerns small, controlled Boolean-task MLPs and a one-dimensional toy vision task, not large language or image-classification models. Several plotted results are described qualitatively in the text without exact values. The proposed local-minima explanation for polysemanticity below capacity is a hypothesis, not a separately tested cause.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted task-specific results on formula reconstruction, code-based classification error, OR/CNF transformations, and other coding-pattern statistics where the paper did not report a separate result directly measuring polysemanticity or its relation to capacity.

untested.parts: No image classifiers; the 1D consecutive-four task is a toy and does not test neuron responses to unrelated image inputs.

No setting where features clearly exceed neurons while polysemanticity is measured. In the sweeps, networks fail once clauses exceed hidden width, and the authors say they do not achieve superposition.
Specific causes (initialization, regularization, training noise) are not isolated. The authors offer a local-minima-count hypothesis without testing it.
No comparison of activation functions, architectures or regularizers.

missing.what: Two-clause (3P1N) DNF network with 16 hidden neurons: positive codes for the two clauses overlap in neurons 1 and 3, polysemanticity far below capacity
Average pairwise code overlap of 4P coding rows across clause counts for j=16, 32, 64, including k below j

record.verdict_notes: Reader's 'supports V3' from r2–r7 is removed, since those rows do not measure polysemanticity. Reader's 'challenges V3' is downgraded to limits_scope, since one sub-capacity case qualifies superposition as a universal cause rather than showing it absent where it should hold. r9 and r10 give only indirect evidence; their accuracy values are task performance.

versions.untested_parts: The one-dimensional pattern-matching task is not an image classifier and does not test whether neurons in image classifiers respond to several unrelated image inputs.
No transformer language models, MLP language-model neurons, or token/context responses are tested.
The paper studies small Boolean-task MLPs, not whether this mechanism explains polysemanticity across trained networks generally.
The paper observes polysemantic coding when the reported feature count is below the hidden width, but does not isolate initialization, regularization, or training noise as causes.
No controlled comparison of activation functions, architectures, or regularizers is reported.
The paper does not investigate whether canonical mixed-response neurons detect a single shared feature or related variants of one job.
The paper does not compare activation-range choices or explanation-scoring methods for classifying neurons as polysemantic.

rows.subject: Two-layer MLP trained on a randomly chosen 8-clause pairwise-AND formula
rows.operation_detail: Inspected the learned first-layer weights and responses in relation to the formula's AND features.
rows.measure: Features to which neuron 4 responds positively
rows.value: Neuron 4 responds positively to four AND features: (x3 ∧ x11), (x0 ∧ x4), (x7 ∧ x15), and (x1 ∧ x14).
rows.note: The authors explicitly describe this as polysemanticity. The reported 8 clauses are fewer than the 16 first-layer neurons.
rows.check: Link and state are correct. The study observes polysemanticity (neuron 4 codes four AND features) with 8 features on 16 neurons, so it is not a superposition regime. For V3, this is a case where the stated cause is absent, yet the effect appears.

rows.subject: Single-hidden-layer MLP trained on the consecutive-four one-dimensional pattern-matching task
rows.operation_detail: Measured overlap among extracted positive-witness codes for four-consecutive-one features.

conditions.value: 40 per reported single run for the code-extraction example

rows.measure: Average number of overlapping coding rows between feature codes
rows.note: The paper reports an average of 12.77 coding rows per possible positive example and states that codes overlap. It does not report the total number of distinct features for this task.
rows.check: Overlap of 2.35 coding rows shows neurons shared across features. The note wrongly says the feature count is unreported: features are the 125 possible start positions of four consecutive ones. Only 70 unique positive coding rows serve them, so this is near or over capacity, and the row cannot separate superposition from non-capacity causes. Not a V4 case.

rows.subject: Two-output single-hidden-layer MLP trained on two DNF formulas
rows.operation_detail: Inspected the learned weight patterns for feature-channel coding across two outputs.
rows.value: The authors report clear feature-channel coding; test-set accuracy with both output bits correct was 97.30%.
rows.note: The authors describe shared hidden neurons as coding for clauses; the total stated clause count is below the hidden width.
rows.check: 16 clauses on 32 neurons, so below capacity, but neuron sharing across clauses is not quantified. The 97.30% value is task accuracy, not a polysemanticity measure.

rows.subject: Three-output single-hidden-layer MLP trained on three DNF formulas
rows.operation_detail: Inspected the learned weight patterns for feature-channel coding across three outputs.
rows.value: The authors report clear feature-channel coding; test-set accuracy with all 3 outputs correct was 95.05%.
rows.note: The authors report that the positive coding rows are not all cleanly assigned to one output; the model has 3 negative rows, or 4 counting row 19.
rows.check: 24 clauses on 32 neurons, but polysemanticity is not quantified. The 95.05% value is task accuracy. The text notes some rows (e.g., neuron 27) do not commit to one output.
